description: The Victorian novel, its 19th-century travel craze, and how a modern adaptation reframes it.
content_html:
Two Worlds, One Journey

Around the World in 80 Days exists in two historical moments simultaneously. Jules Verne published the novel in 1872, feeding a Victorian appetite for global adventure at the precise moment when industrial technology had made such adventure feasible. Laura Eason’s stage adaptation premiered in 2013 at a theatre in the north of England, for a 21st-century audience well aware of what empire had meant and where the “adventure” of Victorian global reach had led. Understanding both contexts is essential not because examiners will ask you to reproduce biographical facts, but because context shapes every staging choice a modern production might make — from the style of the physical theatre to the way the ensemble performs the non-European characters. Both Verne’s world and Eason’s inform what happens on stage.

Jules Verne and the Victorian Moment

Jules Verne (1828–1905) was a French novelist and one of the founders of adventure fiction as a genre. He was fascinated by science and technology, and his novels are populated by engineers, explorers, submarines and balloons — the machines of a world in which human ingenuity was transforming the possible. Around the World in 80 Days was published in 1872, serialised in a French newspaper before appearing as a novel. It arrived at a specific historical junction: the Suez Canal had opened in 1869, dramatically shortening the sea journey between Europe and India; the American transcontinental railroad, also completed in 1869, had linked the Atlantic and Pacific coasts. Together these two engineering achievements made Verne’s premise credible — a journey that would have taken six months was now theoretically achievable in eighty days.

The novel’s popularity was also driven by a specifically Victorian cultural obsession with time. The Great Exhibition of 1851 had celebrated industrial progress and the mastery of nature through technology; by the 1870s, standardised railway time was replacing local time across Britain, the telegraph was sending messages faster than any human traveller, and the world was being divided into predictable time zones. Fogg’s devotion to his schedule is not a character quirk — it is a satirical portrait of Victorian industrial modernity, where the precision of the timetable had become a cultural value.

Key Fact

Verne wrote his novel in 1872, shortly after the Suez Canal (1869) and the transcontinental railroad (1869) made circumnavigation in 80 days theoretically possible. The Victorian obsession with time, schedules and industrial progress gave Fogg’s character its cultural meaning.

The Novel's Colonial Assumptions

Verne’s novel is a product of French and European imperial culture. The world outside Europe functions as spectacular terrain for Fogg’s determination. India, China, Japan and America appear as a series of exotic episodes, each offering a different flavour of drama or comedy. Verne writes with genuine curiosity about these places, but his gaze is consistently that of the European traveller: the cultures he describes are observed from the outside. This is not a unique failing of Verne — it was the dominant mode of 19th-century travel writing, in which the world was divided into the civilised (European) traveller and the colourful (non-European) spectacle. A modern student reading the novel will notice this immediately; a modern director staging the play must decide how to handle it.

Victorian adventure fiction as a genre typically features: a Western (usually British or French) protagonist whose ingenuity and stoicism are tested by the world; a loyal, comic companion who provides the audience’s emotional reaction; a series of exotic locations each with its own distinctive “character”; and a resolution that confirms the protagonist’s superiority through success. Verne’s novel fits this template closely, which is why Eason’s adaptation can engage with both the pleasure of the genre and the questions a modern audience brings to it. The physical-theatre form Eason writes for — eight actors explicitly constructing the world — is itself a kind of comment on the genre: by making the construction visible, the production invites the audience to watch the storytelling as storytelling, rather than being absorbed unquestioningly into the colonial adventure. This is the same principle as alienation effect in epic theatre: the ensemble’s visible transformations remind the audience that they are watching a story, not experiencing reality.

Laura Eason and the 2013 Stage Adaptation

Laura Eason is an American playwright, known in Britain for her work with the New Vic Theatre in Newcastle-under-Lyme. Her adaptation was commissioned specifically for the New Vic’s in-the-round space, directed by Theresa Heskins. This matters for staging: an in-the-round space requires a very different approach from a proscenium arch. There is no “upstage” as a place of exit or hiding; there is no wing space for surprise entrances; every costume change, every physical transformation, every blocking choice must work from every angle. The play Eason wrote is inseparable from this production context: the episodic multi-roling structure, the physical-theatre vocabulary, the use of minimal set and maximum performer ingenuity, all emerge from the demands of that space.

Eason’s adaptation is firmly in the tradition of physical theatre. The influence of companies like Complicite (founded 1983) and Frantic Assembly (founded 1994) is visible in the script’s demands: performers are asked to become not just multiple characters but multiple objects and environments. This ensemble physical-theatre tradition sits comfortably alongside the Brechtian concept of the visible storyteller — the performer who steps out to narrate, to comment, to address the audience directly, making the theatrical fiction visible rather than concealing it behind a naturalistic fourth wall.

Key Fact

Eason’s script draws on the physical-theatre traditions of Complicite (founded 1983) and Frantic Assembly (founded 1994), whose ensemble work — object transformation, bodies-as-environments, ensemble storytelling — underpins the play’s staging demands.

A student who understands both historical contexts can answer a context question with precision. For example: a 12-mark question asking how the historical context shapes a director’s choices for the India scenes might draw on three facts — (1) Verne wrote these scenes from a colonial gaze; (2) Eason adapted the play for a post-colonial 21st-century audience; (3) the physical-theatre form (visible transformation, ensemble storytelling) allows a modern production to handle this material critically without pausing the adventure. The directorial choice that follows from this context might be: the ensemble perform Indian characters with specific, researched gestus — a particular posture, a specific movement quality — that communicates genuine cultural specificity, not a tourist’s impression. This is a contextually informed staging choice, which is exactly what examiners reward at the highest band.
exam_tip_html: Context questions require you to connect historical or theatrical facts directly to staging choices — not simply to list them. A common mistake is writing two paragraphs about Victorian history and Verne’s biography and then adding “this would affect the director’s choices” without specifying how. The examiner needs to see the link made explicit: “Because Verne wrote from within a colonial culture, a modern director staging the India scenes would need to make deliberate choices to give Indian characters their own specificity — for example, using a researched gestus for each character rather than generic physical caricature.” That is a contextually grounded staging answer. For the 12-mark analyse-intentions question, always move from context to intention to specific staging choice to audience effect — four steps, every time.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Verne wrote in 1872 when the Suez Canal and the transcontinental railroad had made circumnavigation in 80 days newly possible — Fogg’s schedule-obsession reflects Victorian industrial culture, not personal eccentricity.
  • Eason’s 2013 adaptation for the New Vic’s in-the-round space draws on the physical-theatre traditions of Complicite and Frantic Assembly — the in-the-round configuration directly shapes the play’s staging demands.
  • Understanding both historical contexts allows a director to make informed choices about how to handle Verne’s colonial gaze — using gestus, costume and soundscape to give non-European characters specificity and dignity.

practice_questions.text: In which year was Jules Verne's novel Around the World in 80 Days first published?
What is meant by 'physical theatre' as a theatrical tradition?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that physical theatre emphasises storytelling through physical movement, ensemble creation or imagination; 1 mark for explaining that it typically foregrounds the performer's body as the primary storytelling tool, often with minimal set and visible transformation.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the in-the-round staging configuration at the New Vic shapes the demands placed on the performers in Around the World in 80 Days.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification that in-the-round means the audience surrounds the performance area on all sides (1); explanation that there is no 'upstage' as a place of exit or concealment and no wing space (1); a specific staging demand that follows from this (e.g. every physical transformation must be visible and legible from every angle; costume changes must be made in full view; blocking must constantly work from multiple directions) (1); explanation of how this connects to the play's physical-theatre ensemble form (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how knowledge of Verne's 1872 historical context might shape a director's choices for staging a non-European location in Around the World in 80 Days.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the relevant historical context (Victorian colonial gaze; non-European locations presented as exotic backdrop in Verne's novel) (1); explanation that a modern director is aware this framing is now problematic (1); a specific staging or design choice that responds to this context (e.g. using researched costume elements to give characters cultural specificity; building a soundscape from authentic musical textures for each location) (1); explanation of how this choice communicates something different to a modern audience than Verne's original framing intended (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Eason's 2013 stage adaptation uses the physical-theatre tradition to both celebrate Verne's adventure story and create a production that a modern audience can engage with critically.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response analyses Eason's use of physical theatre (ensemble multi-roling, object transformation, visible storytelling) as a deliberate formal choice that serves two purposes simultaneously: it honours the adventure genre's energy and pace, keeping every episode kinetic and theatrical, while the visible construction of the world (performers explicitly becoming objects, locations and minor characters) invites the audience to watch the storytelling as storytelling rather than being absorbed unquestioningly into the colonial adventure narrative. The alienation effect created by visible transformation is connected to Brecht's tradition of making theatre's mechanics visible. The response analyses specific staging moments (e.g. the ensemble physically creating the steam engine) as both thrilling spectacle and implicit reminder that this is a constructed story. A judgment is made about whether Eason achieves both goals successfully.
Secure: The dual function of physical theatre is identified and mostly analysed; at least one specific staging moment referenced; the connection to both adventure and modern audience engagement is generally clear.
Developing: Physical theatre is described but its function in relation to the colonial theme is not analysed; the staging moment may be general rather than specific.
Emerging: Describes physical theatre without connecting it to Eason's intentions or the audience's critical engagement.

practice_questions.text: You are directing Around the World in 80 Days for a contemporary audience. Discuss how you would use staging configuration, physical theatre, lighting and costume to communicate both the Victorian context and a modern perspective on the story. Refer to specific design and performance choices in at least two scenes.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The response makes clear directorial choices grounded in both historical contexts. For the Victorian context: costume choices (e.g. Fogg's fixed Victorian frock coat and pocket watch as the anchoring symbol of industrial time; Reform Club gentlemen in identical black with top hats, moving in synchronised tableau to communicate their conformity and social rigidity). For the modern perspective: physical-theatre choices that make the construction visible (e.g. the ensemble visibly preparing each location before Fogg arrives, signalling to the audience that the world is being made, not simply inhabited); in a specific non-European scene, researched costume elements and a culturally specific soundscape that give the location genuine texture. Lighting choices for both Victorian and non-European scenes are named (e.g. cool, sharp profile lantern for the Reform Club; a warmer, wider wash with more directional side-light for the Indian scenes to suggest a different quality of light without caricature). The in-the-round configuration is discussed with reference to sightlines and the impact on blocking. A unified directorial vision is clearly stated and sustained.
Secure: At least three elements covered with concrete choices; both historical contexts are referenced; two scenes addressed; a directorial intention is present.
Developing: Some concrete choices; fewer than three elements in detail; one or both historical contexts may not be addressed through specific staging choices.
Emerging: General ideas about staging and context without concrete choices or connection between the two.

knowledge_checks.q: In which year did the Suez Canal open, making Fogg's 80-day journey theoretically possible?
Where did Eason's stage adaptation of Around the World in 80 Days premiere in 2013?
Eason's adaptation draws on the physical-theatre traditions of Complicite and _____ Assembly.
In Brecht's epic theatre, the _____ effect prevents the audience from losing themselves in empathy and encourages them to think critically.
Match each contextual fact to its staging implication:
right: Requires directors to give non-European characters specific, researched gestus and costume rather than generic exoticism
Every blocking and transformation choice must be visible and legible from all sides — no wings, no hiding
Performers become not just characters but environments and objects, making the construction of the story visible

flashcard_questions.q: When was Jules Verne's Around the World in 80 Days first published?
flashcard_questions.a: 1872, serialised in a French newspaper before publication as a novel.

flashcard_questions.q: What two engineering achievements opened in 1869 made Fogg's journey newly possible?
flashcard_questions.a: The Suez Canal and the American transcontinental railroad.

flashcard_questions.q: Who adapted Around the World in 80 Days for the stage in 2013?
flashcard_questions.a: Laura Eason, commissioned by the New Vic Theatre, Newcastle-under-Lyme.

flashcard_questions.q: Who directed the world premiere of Eason's adaptation?
What is the in-the-round staging configuration?
flashcard_questions.a: A configuration where the audience surrounds the performance area on all sides.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a proscenium arch staging configuration?
flashcard_questions.a: A configuration where the audience faces a stage framed by a large rectangular arch, like a picture frame.

flashcard_questions.q: What is physical theatre as a tradition?
flashcard_questions.a: A theatre-making approach using physical movement, ensemble creation and imagination rather than text-heavy realistic staging.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two physical-theatre companies whose work underpins Eason's staging approach.

flashcard_questions.a: A theatrical technique that prevents the audience losing themselves in empathy and encourages critical thinking.

flashcard_questions.q: What is gestus in the context of this play?
flashcard_questions.a: A physical attitude communicating a character's social status instantly, used especially for multi-roled minor characters.

flashcard_questions.q: What was Verne's cultural context when writing the novel?
flashcard_questions.a: Victorian imperial culture — the world outside Europe served as exotic backdrop for the European protagonist's journey.
The choreographed arrangement of performers on stage at any given moment.

glossary_terms.definition: Brecht's term for a theatrical effect that prevents the audience losing themselves in empathy and instead encourages them to think critically about what they are seeing.
A staging configuration in which the audience surrounds the performance area on all sides, requiring all performer choices to be visible from every direction.
A staging configuration in which the audience faces a stage framed by a large rectangular arch, with the performers and set visible as if through a picture frame.
The choreographed arrangement of performers on stage at any given moment.
A theatre-making approach that emphasises storytelling through physical movement, ensemble creation and imagination rather than text-heavy realistic staging.
A physical attitude or stance that communicates a character's social status and role in a single, instantly readable physical image.
